'''Donnie Lewis Edwards Jr.''' (born April 6, 1973) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for 13 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and [[San Diego Chargers]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://passtheword.wordpress.com/2006/11/24/tony-romo-uno-caliente-hombre/ |title= Tony Romo: Uno Caliente Hombre|website=passtheword.wordpress.com |date= November 24, 2006|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130324010908/https://passtheword.wordpress.com/2006/11/24/tony-romo-uno-caliente-hombre/ |archive-date=March 24, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Easton Jr. |first=Edward |date=2024-06-03 |title=Former Chief Donnie Edwards: 'I never wanted to leave Kansas City' |url=https://chiefswire.usatoday.com/2024/06/03/donnie-edwards-never-wanted-leave-kansas-city/ |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=Chiefs Wire |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Summers |first=Joe |date=2024-06-05 |title=Former Chiefs Standout Reveals He 'Never Wanted to Leave Kansas City' |url=https://kckingdom.com/posts/former-chiefs-standout-reveals-never-wanted-leave-kansas-city-01hzmabbzgtn |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=KC Kingdom |language=en-US}}</ref>  He played [[college football]] for the [[UCLA Bruins football|UCLA Bruins]], earning third-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors in 1994. He was selected by the Chiefs in the fourth round of the [[1996 NFL draft]].

Edwards retired as one of only eight players in the history of the NFL to record more than 20 [[interception]]s and 20 [[quarterback sack|sacks]] during his career.<ref name="10news.com">{{Cite web |url=http://10news.com/about/10news-leadership-award-winner-donnie-edwards |title=10News Leadership Award Winner Donnie Edwards - 10News.com KGTV ABC10 San Diego |access-date=June 16, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141101053020/http://www.10news.com/about/10news-leadership-award-winner-donnie-edwards |archive-date=November 1, 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Since his retirement in 2009, Edwards has devoted himself to philanthropic work with the Best Defense Foundation and children from underprivileged backgrounds.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blackanthem.com/News/International_21/NFL_Players_Visit_Injured_Troops_in_Kuwait5819.shtml |title=Archived copy |access-date=June 16, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151225093839/http://blackanthem.com/News/International_21/NFL_Players_Visit_Injured_Troops_in_Kuwait5819.shtml |archive-date=December 25, 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/sdut-athletes-provide-a-charge-for-kids-2004mar03-story.html |title=Athletes provide a charge for kids |last1=Frank |first1=Jeff |date=March 3, 2004 |newspaper=San Diego Union Tribute |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151225195235/https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/news/2004/Mar/03/athletes-provide-a-charge-for-kids/ |archive-date=December 25, 2015 |access-date=January 15, 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref>

He played [[college football]] for the [[Pacific Tigers football|Pacific Tigers]] and [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford Cardinal]]. Spragan was signed by the [[New Orleans Saints]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 1999.  He was also a member of the [[Green Bay Packers]], [[Cleveland Browns]], [[Denver Broncos]], [[Miami Dolphins]], and [[Buffalo Bills]].

'''Donnie Shell''' (born August 26, 1952) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (football position)|safety]] for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) between 1974 and 1987. Shell was a member of the Steelers famed [[Steel Curtain]] defense in the 1970s.

Shell retired as the NFL strong safety career leader in [[interception]]s with 51. He started 11 consecutive seasons for the Steelers and was selected to the Steelers All-Time Team, the [[College Football Hall of Fame]], the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] (Class of 2020), and to the NFL Silver Anniversary Super Bowl Team.

'''Donnell Woolford''' (born January 6, 1966) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily with the [[Chicago Bears]]. He was selected by the Bears in the first round (11th overall) of the [[1989 NFL draft]]. Woolford played 10 seasons for the Bears from 1989 to 1997, the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] from 1997 to 1998 and [[Carolina Panthers]] from 1998 to 1999. He was a [[Pro Bowl]] selection in 1994. Woolford was surpassed by [[Charles Tillman]] for the most interceptions by a Bears cornerback, although Donnell achieved the goal 18 games faster than Tillman.<ref>{{cite web |last=Mayer |first=Larry |url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Tillman-repeats-stellar-performance/cd4329ee-7829-43f1-8286-e2262d28f33d |title=Tillman repeats stellar performance |publisher=[[Chicago Bears]] |access-date=October 8, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121011012951/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Tillman-repeats-stellar-performance/cd4329ee-7829-43f1-8286-e2262d28f33d |archive-date=October 11, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Player Bio|url=http://www.chicagobears.com/team/roster/charles-tillman/d7f42114-9660-47bd-8107-58b4bee810c9/|publisher=Chicago Bears|access-date=November 19, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121104155328/http://www.chicagobears.com/team/roster/charles-tillman/d7f42114-9660-47bd-8107-58b4bee810c9/|archive-date=November 4, 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> Woolford was a graduate of [[Douglas Byrd High School]] in Fayetteville, NC and [[Clemson University]].<!--This reference is combined with the story to show that Tillman has surpassed Woolford.-->

'''Donald Ray Gibbs''' was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[Punter (football)|punter]] who played college football for [[TCU Horned Frogs football|TCU Horned Frogs]] and played professionally for the [[New Orleans Saints]] of the [[National Football League|NFL]].

Gibbs born on December 31, 1945, to Clyde and Frances Gibbs.<ref name=obit/>  He played high school football at [[Tyler Legacy High School|Robert E. Lee High School]] where he not only punted but also played [[quarterback]].<ref name=obit/><ref name=kick/>  In 1963 he led Robert E. Lee to its first winning record in football.<ref name=obit/>  In 1965 he won the Troy V. Post Award as "1965 Young Texan of the Year."<ref name=obit/><ref name=kick>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|newspaper=Fort Worth Star-Telegram|author=Moore, Dick|title=Donnie has kick(s) coming|date=September 11, 1965|page=2|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107907446/fort-worth-star-telegram/}}</ref>

Gibbs said of becoming TCU's punter "I feel like a freak, standing off to one side of the field and just kicking the ball. It's a little boring and I miss playing quarterback. But if this is the best way I can help the team, then I'm for it.<ref name=kick/>  At TCU Gibbs was not only the team's punter but also the [[holder (gridiron football)|holder]] for [[placekicker]] [[Bruce Alford Jr.|Bruce Alford]].  Alford, who played several years in the NFL, said of Gibbs "Donnie knows just how I like the ball to sit.  He has sure, quick hands and takes the snap and gets it down in a hurry...It's like a [[quarterback]] who gets used to taking a snapback from one [[Center (gridiron football)|center]].  It sure would upset me if I didn't have Donnie."<ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|newspaper=Fort Worth Star-Telegram|author=Trinkle, Jim|date=September 7, 1966|title=Best foot in Frog football|pages=1-D–2-D|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107906223/fort-worth-star-telegram/}}</ref>  In 1966, he was named to the ''[[Fort Worth Star-Telegram]]'' All-[[Southwest Conference]] Team after recording a 43.1 yard per punt average through 9 games.<ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|newspaper=Fort Worth Star-Telegram|author=Trinkle, Jim|date=November 27, 1966|page=3-B|title=Four sophs make S-T's All-SWC|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107906728/fort-worth-star-telegram/}}</ref>  After college Gibbs played quarterback and punter for the [[Fort Worth Braves]] of the [[Texas Football League]] from 1968 through 1971.<ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|newspaper=Longview News-Journal|author=Thomas, Van|title=Braves will meet Lake Charles here tonight|date=July 26, 1969|page=1-B|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107909112/longview-news-journal/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107909421/fort-worth-star-telegram/|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|title=6 Braves named all-stars|work=Fort Worth Star-Telegram |date=January 9, 1971|page=4-C}}</ref>

Gibbs played for the Saints in 1974.  He asked for a tryout as a 29 year old and beat out [[Steve O'Neal]] – holder of the NFL record for longest punt ever – for the punting job.<ref name=gift/><ref name=snap>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|newspaper=Pensacola News Journal|pages=1C–2C|title=Gibbs' muffed punt snap draws North's criticism|author=Palmer, Al|date=September 16, 1974|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107905554/pensacola-news-journal/}}</ref>  Gibbs had spent the prior two years selling women's clothing.<ref name=snap/>  His first game with the Saints was against the [[San Francisco 49ers]] and started well as he executed two [[Coffin corner (American football)|coffin corner]] kicks to pin the 49ers deep in their own zone.<ref name=snap/>  But disaster struck late in the game when he [[fumble]]d a perfect snap to set up the 49ers' winning score.<ref name=gift>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|newspaper=Hattiesburg American|author=Cleveland, Rick|title=49ers take 17-13 Saints gift|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107902630/hattiesburg-american/|page=11|date=September 16, 1974}}</ref><ref name=snap/><ref name=flat>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|newspaper=Shreveport Journal|date=September 20, 1974|page=B7|author=Griffin, Bob|title=Gibbs Just Flat Dropped the Ball|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107910097/the-shreveport-journal/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|newspaper=Shreveport Journal|title=All Saints Needed Was a Kick in the End|author=Byrd, Jerry|date=September 16, 1974|page=1C|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107911511/the-shreveport-journal/}}</ref>  Gibbs said of the play "I just flat dropped it. I wasn't concentrating on fielding the snap. I went in there and didn't do my first job, catch the ball."<ref name=flat/>  He was waived by the Saints before their next game and replaced by veteran [[Tom Blanchard]].<ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|newspaper=Clarion-Ledger|title=Saints drop Donnie Gibbs|page=4|date=September 20, 1974|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107903209/clarion-ledger/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-08-19|newspaper=South Idaho Press|title=Saints replace Donnie Gibbs|date=September 20, 1974|page=6|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107910508/south-idaho-press/}}</ref>
